result:
The proposed answer is almost certainly wrong, mainly because step 4 is unjustified.

Step 4 claims, with no proof, that the spectral extremal graph is a complete bipartite graph. A complete bipartite graph K_{k+1,n-k-1} has spectral radius √((k+1)(n-k-1)), which is of order √(kn).

A graph that is nearly complete does much better. Nash-Williams–Tutte says τ(G) < k forces a partition into p parts with fewer than k(p-1) crossing edges. Since G is (k+1)-edge-connected, p = 2 is impossible, so p ≥ 3. The extremal graph should therefore be a large clique with a few small attached parts, joined by at most about 2k-1 crossing edges. Its spectral radius is about n minus a constant, far above √(kn).

So K_{k+1,n-k-1} cannot be the maximizer. Its edge count (k+1)(n-k-1) is linear in n, while the true extremal graph has roughly C(n-c,2) edges, quadratic in n.

I have not derived the exact extremal graph or its edge count. The bipartite claim is nonetheless contradicted by the comparison above, so the final answer is incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
